title: Circular Queue (Ring Buffer)
description: Modulo wrap-around, front/rear sentinel -1, full vs. empty detection, and ring traces on the CircularQueue used by circular-queue.html.

questions.prompt: Why does a circular queue advance rear using (rear + 1) mod capacity instead of rear + 1?
choices: So rear wraps back to index 0 and reuses freed slots at the front, preventing false overflow
So elements stay sorted in ascending order inside the array
So the array automatically doubles its capacity when full
So dequeue can remove elements from the rear in O(1) time
questions.answer: So rear wraps back to index 0 and reuses freed slots at the front, preventing false overflow
questions.explanation: Modulo arithmetic connects index capacity - 1 back to index 0 so new enqueues reuse slots vacated by earlier dequeues, eliminating linear-queue false overflow. Automatically doubling capacity is a tempting distractor from dynamic arrays, whereas a circular ring buffer keeps a fixed size.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 4, enqueue 4 values, dequeue the front value, then enqueue again to watch rear wrap to [0].

questions.prompt: In CircularQueue on circular-queue.html, an empty ring is represented by front = -1 and rear = -1.
questions.explanation: CircularQueue reserves front = -1 (with rear = -1) as its empty sentinel, and sets front = rear = 0 on the first enqueue. Answering False is tempting if you recall LinearQueue's front = 0, rear = -1; in a circular queue that would make (-1 + 1) mod n == 0 == front, falsely triggering the full condition when empty.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 5 and read the status banner showing front = rear = -1.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 4. You enqueue 10, 20, 30, 40, dequeue once (removing 10), and then enqueue 50. List the logical queue from front to rear.
questions.hint: 50 wraps into array index 0, but which index is front?
questions.explanation: Dequeue removes 10 from index 0 and moves front to 1. Enqueue 50 wraps rear to (3 + 1) mod 4 = 0, so the backing array is [50, 20, 30, 40], but logical FIFO order starts at front = 1 and walks around: 20, 30, 40, 50. Answering "50, 20, 30, 40" reads physical index 0 first instead of starting at front.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 4, enqueue 10, 20, 30, 40, dequeue 10, then enqueue 50.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of enqueue(x) and dequeue() on CircularQueue?
questions.explanation: Both enqueue and dequeue perform a constant number of checks, one modulo index calculation (i + 1) mod n, and one array write, so both take O(1) time regardless of capacity. O(n) is tempting if you imagine shifting elements back to index 0 on wrap-around, which modulo indexing avoids.

questions.prompt: On circular-queue.html, which capacity value is rejected by Allocate Ring?
questions.explanation: CircularQueue.MIN_CAPACITY is 2 and MAX_CAPACITY is 100, so capacity 1 is rejected while 2, 10, and 100 are accepted. Picking 100 is tempting if you confuse this limit with stack.html (max 12) or priority-queue.html (max 50), and picking 2 forgets that 2 is the smallest valid ring size.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: type 1 into Capacity (2-100) and press Allocate Ring.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 5 (indices 0 to 4). You enqueue 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, dequeue twice (removing 1 and 2), and then enqueue 6 and 7. What is the rear index afterwards?
questions.hint: Apply (rear + 1) mod 5 for each of the last two enqueues starting from rear = 4.
questions.explanation: After enqueuing 1 through 5, rear = 4. Two dequeues move front from 0 to 2 while rear stays 4. Enqueuing 6 wraps rear = (4 + 1) mod 5 = 0, and enqueuing 7 moves rear = (0 + 1) mod 5 = 1. Answering 6 forgets to take mod 5; answering 0 stops after only one wrap step.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 5, enqueue 1-5, dequeue 1 and 2, enqueue 6 and 7, then press Rear (Last).

questions.prompt: In this visualizer's CircularQueue, one array slot must always stay empty to tell full from empty, so a ring of capacity 5 can hold at most 4 items.
questions.explanation: Because CircularQueue uses front = -1 exclusively for the empty state, all 5 slots can be occupied and (rear + 1) mod 5 == front unambiguously signals full. Answering True is very tempting because an alternative ring-buffer convention (using front == rear for empty) does sacrifice one slot—but this implementation uses all capacity slots.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 5, enqueue 5 values, and click Queue Size and IsFull?.

questions.prompt: Which conditions are always TRUE for a full CircularQueue of capacity n (where n >= 2)? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: A full ring holds all n elements (size == n), is non-empty (front != -1), and has rear immediately before front around the circle ((rear + 1) mod n == front). front == rear means only 1 element is stored (impossible when full with n >= 2), and rear == n - 1 only holds when front == 0, not after wrap-around.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 6, with front = 4 and rear = 1. How many elements are currently stored in the queue?
questions.hint: Use ((rear - front + n) mod n) + 1, or list the occupied indices starting at 4 and wrapping past 5 to 1.
questions.explanation: Walking clockwise from front = 4 to rear = 1 visits indices 4, 5, 0, and 1—4 elements in total, matching ((1 - 4 + 6) mod 6) + 1 = 4. Answering 3 drops the + 1 (off-by-one); answering -2 uses rear - front + 1 without adding capacity n before taking mod 6.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 6, enqueue 1-6, dequeue 1-4, enqueue 7 and 8, then press Queue Size.

questions.prompt: On circular-queue.html, a ring of capacity 4 holds only one element 77 at index 2 (front = 2, rear = 2). You type 77 in the dequeue box and click Dequeue. What are front and rear afterwards?
questions.explanation: Because front == rear, 77 was the sole remaining element, so CircularQueue.dequeue() resets both pointers to -1 (empty). Choosing front = 3 and rear = 2 is the most tempting mistake: advancing front to (2 + 1) mod 4 = 3 would leave (rear + 1) mod 4 == front, making an empty ring look full! front = 0, rear = -1 is LinearQueue's empty state, not CircularQueue's.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 4, enqueue 1, 2, 77, dequeue 1 and 2 so 77 sits at [2], then dequeue 77.

questions.prompt: A circular queue has capacity 4 (indices 0 to 3). You run: enqueue 1, enqueue 2, enqueue 3, enqueue 4, dequeue, dequeue, enqueue 5, dequeue, dequeue. What is the front index afterwards?
questions.hint: Remember that front also wraps around with (front + 1) mod 4 when moving past index 3.
questions.explanation: After enqueuing 1-4, front = 0 and rear = 3. Two dequeues advance front to 2, and enqueue 5 wraps rear to 0. Two more dequeues remove 3 (front = 3) and 4 (front = (3 + 1) mod 4 = 0), wrapping front to index 0 where 5 remains. Answering 4 forgets modulo wrap on front; answering -1 wrongly assumes all 5 items were dequeued.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 4, enqueue 1-4, dequeue 1 and 2, enqueue 5, dequeue 3 and 4, then press Peek (Front).

questions.prompt: In a circular queue, rear is always greater than or equal to front whenever the queue is non-empty.
questions.explanation: As soon as rear wraps past capacity - 1 back to index 0 while front > 0, rear is strictly smaller than front even though the queue is valid and non-empty (for example, capacity 4 with front = 2 and rear = 0). Answering True is tempting because rear >= front is always true in a LinearQueue where indices never wrap.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 4, enqueue 1-4, dequeue 1, enqueue 5, and observe front = 1 while rear = 0.

questions.prompt: What is the time complexity of toArray() on CircularQueue to return all n currently stored elements in front-to-rear order?
questions.explanation: toArray() starts at front and advances idx = (idx + 1) mod capacity exactly size (= n) times, copying each element once in O(n) time. O(1) is tempting because size, peek, and peekRear are O(1), but enumerating all n items requires visiting every stored element.

questions.prompt: Starting from an empty CircularQueue of capacity 3, you execute: enqueue 10, enqueue 20, enqueue 30, dequeue, enqueue 40, enqueue 50. Which statements are TRUE afterwards? Select all that apply.
choices: enqueue(50) fails with a queue overflow
answer: enqueue(50) fails with a queue overflow
questions.explanation: Dequeuing 10 frees index 0 and moves front to 1. Enqueuing 40 wraps rear to (2 + 1) mod 3 = 0, giving slots [40, 20, 30] with front = 1, rear = 0; since (0 + 1) mod 3 == 1 == front, isFull() is true and enqueue(50) overflows. peek() is 20 (at front = 1), not 40 (at index 0 / rear), and front is 1 rather than 0.
questions.page: On circular-queue.html: allocate capacity 3, enqueue 10, 20, 30, dequeue 10, enqueue 40, then try to enqueue 50.
